sections.h2: Selling in Monroe Township, Gloucester County
sections.html:
Monroe Township in Gloucester County, the Williamstown ZIP 08094 township, runs a resale certificate of occupancy inspection that the buyer's paperwork must accompany. Population is about 38,137 and the township counts 14,116 households of about 2.65 people. Owners live in 85.2 percent of homes, with a median value of $283,100 and a median household income of $96,980. Workers average 31.7 minutes to their jobs.

The township covers 46.93 square miles, nearly all of it land. Williamstown and Victory Lakes are the census designated places, and Berryland, Broad Lane, Cecil, Cross Keys, Downer, New Brooklyn and Radix are other place names you may see on a deed or listing.

The Monroe Township Housing Office requires a resale certificate of occupancy application, and the township asks for it 3 to 4 weeks before settlement. A completed inspection is valid for only 60 days. The office is at 125 Virginia Avenue in Williamstown, reachable at 856-728-9800 ext. 289 or 296, and applications go in person or by mail.

Monroe Township Housing resale fees.
Fee typeAmount
Resale inspection application$200
Request made less than 7 business days ahead$300

Reinspection requested less than 7 business days ahead$50

Failure to obtain the resale certificate of occupancy$300

Payment must be exact cash, a check or a money order payable to Monroe Township Housing. The office does not take credit or debit cards, and every fee is non-refundable. The buyer must also complete a notarized Acknowledgement of Responsibility, and inspections cannot be scheduled without it.

The township's current checklist lists the full extent of the resale inspection.

  • House numbers at least 3 inches tall, on both sides of the mailbox.
  • Smoke detectors on every level, either ten-year sealed battery units or hardwired units under ten years old, and carbon monoxide detectors outside sleeping areas unless the house is all electric with a detached garage.
  • A 2A-10B:C fire extinguisher mounted and visible when leaving the kitchen, with a service tag from the last 12 months or a receipt for a new one.
  • For private wells, a satisfactory lab report that includes mercury. For private septic systems, a certification from the Gloucester County Department of Health.
  • Pool barriers with a 4 foot fence and a 4 foot gate that opens outward, closes itself and latches with the release 54 inches off the ground, plus working safety straps on hot tubs.
  • All zoning, construction and Board of Health permits and violations closed, and any abandoned property fees or emergency work charges paid.

Section 162-11 of the township code lets a buyer of a dwelling that is unfit at transfer sign an affidavit listing the repairs needed. The affidavit lasts 60 days, work must start right after the sale, and the Housing Official can extend the period only for good cause. The buyer applies for the transfer before the scheduled closing, and can also assume the seller's duty to obtain the certificate by a written waiver filed with the Housing Department.

A certificate is not a warranty. The buyer signs that acknowledgment and accepts responsibility for fixing violations or unpermitted work found later. The form recommends the buyer get a survey no more than 90 days old and file an OPRA request for permits with the Zoning and Construction Offices, and, where it applies, check for Pinelands Commission approval.

The Black Horse Pike crosses the township from northwest to southeast, carrying Route 42 in the northwest part and U.S. Route 322 in the southeast. Buyers who work in the city or at the shore weigh this heavily. Typical drive times run about 30 minutes to Philadelphia and 35 to Atlantic City, and the Atlantic City Expressway runs just outside its border. U.S. 322 on the west side reaches the New Jersey Turnpike in about 30 minutes. NJ Transit buses 315, 400 and 463 serve the area.

Gloucester County uses an alternative assessment calendar, so the Board of Taxation takes appeals from November 15 through January 15, with a 4:00 pm cutoff on the last day for paper or online filings. Assessment postcards are mailed on or before November 15, and paper appeals need a check made out to the Gloucester County Board of Taxation. Online filing accepts credit cards.

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, which rises with the sale price. Deeds are recorded with the Gloucester County Clerk, whose posted fee is $30 for the first page and $10 for each additional page. The Clerk's Office takes only money orders, checks or credit cards, checks of $10,000 or more must be certified, and out-of-state personal checks are not accepted. The recording line is 856-853-3235.

sections.h2: Steps to close a Monroe sale
sections.html:
Timing drives most of this sale, so plan backward from the settlement date. Start by checking the calendar. Apply to the Housing Office 3 to 4 weeks before settlement, and book the visit so the 60-day validity covers your closing date. Pay the fee in the accepted form and confirm the buyer has filed the notarized acknowledgment.

Walk the house with the checklist first. Replace expired smoke detectors, mount the extinguisher where it can be seen from the kitchen door and fix the house numbers. For a private well, order the lab report with the mercury test, and for a septic system arrange the county health certification. Close any open permits, since violations and unpaid emergency work charges must be cleared.

Keep the paperwork together for the buyer's attorney: the inspection result, the well or septic report, the permit closeouts, and the receipt for the extinguisher. Missing documents are a common reason a settlement date moves, and each reinspection or rushed request adds a fee. If you live out of the area, ask the Housing Office whether someone can meet the inspector, because a no-answer visit is charged $50.

If the house needs more work than you can finish, the temporary certificate route and the buyer's repair affidavit are the options to ask about. A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can often use that affidavit, which lets the sale close while repairs follow within the 60 days.

faqs.q: How much is the Monroe Township resale certificate fee?
faqs.a: The township charges $200 for the resale inspection application, or $300 when the request comes less than seven business days before it is needed. A reinspection is $25, and the fees are not refundable.

faqs.q: How early should I apply for a Monroe resale certificate?
faqs.a: Apply 3 to 4 weeks before settlement. The inspection stays valid for 60 days, so time the visit to your settlement date, and file the notarized buyer acknowledgment with the application.

faqs.q: Do I need a well test to sell a Monroe house on a private well?
faqs.a: Yes. The checklist requires a satisfactory lab report that includes mercury for a private well, and a Gloucester County Department of Health certification for a private septic system.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take on repairs after buying a Monroe house?
faqs.a: A buyer can sign an affidavit listing the repairs needed for legal occupancy. It lasts 60 days, repairs must begin right after the sale, and the buyer applies for the transfer before the closing.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Monroe assessment in Gloucester County?
faqs.a: The window runs from November 15 to January 15, and filings must be in by 4:00 pm on January 15. Assessment postcards go out on or before November 15.
